title: Watch Seoul’s 6,500-Year Evolution in a Mesmerizing 3D Animated Time Lapse
content: In this century, few countries have been as visibly successful as South Korea. China’s vertiginous economic rise once absorbed vast amounts of news-media attention, but its soft power has comparatively little reach across the wider world, at least in English-speaking countries. By this point, many if not most Westerners haven’t just eaten Korean food, but also driven a Korean car, heard Korean pop music, or watched a Korean film or TV show. The resulting sense of familiarity can prove deceptive to those who eventually make the trip there, but it does, at least, mark an improvement on the scant knowledge of the place they had before. Not so long ago, they could say little with certainty except this: South Korea’s got Seoul.

title: Inspiration from Charles Bukowski: You Might Be Old, Your Life May Be “Crappy,” But You Can Still Make Good Art
content:
Now more than ever, there’s tremendous pressure to make it big while you’re young.

Pity the 31-year-old who fails to make it onto a 30-under-30 list…

The soon-to-graduate high schooler passed over for YouTube stardom…

The great hordes who creep into middle age without so much as a TED Talk to their names…

Social media definitely magnifies the sensation that an unacceptable number of our peers have been granted first-class cabins aboard a ship that’s sailed without us. If we weren’t so demoralized, we’d sue Instagram for creating the impression that everyone else’s perfectly filtered life is leading to book deals and profiles in The New Yorker.

Don’t despair, dear reader. Charles Bukowski is about to make your day from beyond the grave.

In 1993, at the age of 73, the late writer and self-described “spoiled old toad,” took a break from recording the audiobook of Run With the Hunted to reflect upon his “crappy” life.

Some of these thoughts made it into Drew Christie’s animation, above, a reminder that the smoothest road isn’t always necessarily the richest one.

title: The Painting Nobody Wanted: How Matisse’s The Red Studio Went from a London Nightclub to a Masterpiece of Modern Art
content:
A journalist paid Henri Matisse a visit not long after he’d painted The Red Studio in 1911. “I like it, but I don’t completely understand it,” the artist is quoted as admitting of that latest work. “I like it, but I don’t know why I precisely painted it this way.” The painting was a rendition of the very same Issy-les-Moulineaux studio in which they were talking, though you wouldn’t necessarily recognize it at first glance. Deep red covered two-thirds of its surface, an unorthodox choice that probably contributed to its rejection by Matisse’s loyal patron Sergei Shchukin, who’d commissioned Dance and Music. This departure from strict representation fared no better when it was shown in London, and thereafter at the groundbreaking 1913 “Armory Show” in the United States.

By 1926, when The Red Studio finally made its Paris debut, public sensibilities had begun to catch up with Matisse’s instincts. The following year, it found a buyer in the owner of London’s Gargoyle Club, a favorite haunt of the Bright Young Things, where the painting would hang for more than a decade.

title: When Charles Dickens Met Edgar Allan Poe
content:
“There comes Poe with his raven,” wrote the poet James Russell Lowell in 1848, “like Barnaby Rudge, / Three-fifths of him genius and two-fifths sheer fudge.” Barnaby Rudge, as you may know, is a novel by Charles Dickens, published serially in 1841. Set during the anti-Catholic Gordon Riots of 1780, the book stands as Dickens’ first historical novel and a prelude of sorts to A Tale of Two Cities. But what, you may wonder, does it have to do with Poe and “his raven”?

Quite a lot, it turns out. Poe reviewed the first four chapters of Dickens’ Barnaby Rudge for Graham’s Magazine, predicting the end of the novel and finding out later he was correct when he reviewed it again upon completion. He was particularly taken with one character: a chatty raven named Grip who accompanies the simple-minded Barnaby. Poe described the bird as “intensely amusing,” points out Atlas Obscura, and also wrote that Grip’s “croaking might have been prophetically heard in the course of the drama.”

title: Explore the Reading List for Harvard’s Humanities 10: The “Brutal” Humanities Class That’s Suddenly in High Demand
content: There are plenty of good reasons a student might want to go to Harvard. One is its long history, at least by American standards; another is the formidable accomplishments of the professors hired to teach there. But on some level, a teenager looking to come up in the world — or, in many cases, parents looking to put their teenager up in the world — understands full well that much of what an institution like Harvard offers comes down to its selectivity. Considering how few get in versus how many apply, it would be easy to believe that most of a student’s battle is won at the point of acceptance. Imagine the despair, then, of a newly arrived Harvardian facing another entrance exam and written application just to get a seat in Humanities 10.

title: “Don’t Try”: Charles Bukowski’s Concise Philosophy of Art and Life
content:
In 1994, Charles Bukowski was buried in a Los Angeles cemetery, beneath a simple gravestone. The stone memorializes the poet’s name. It recites his dates of birth and death, but adds the symbol of a boxer between the two, suggesting his life was a struggle. And it adds the very succinct epitaph, “Don’t Try.”

There you have it, Bukowski’s philosophy on art and life boiled down to two words. But what do they mean? Let’s look back at the epistolary record and find out.

In October 1963, Bukowski recounted in a letter to John William Corrington how someone once asked him, “What do you do? How do you write, create?” To which, he replied: “You don’t try. That’s very important: ‘not’ to try, either for Cadillacs, creation or immortality. You wait, and if nothing happens, you wait some more. It’s like a bug high on the wall. You wait for it to come to you. When it gets close enough you reach out, slap out and kill it. Or if you like its looks you make a pet out of it.”

So, the key to life and art, it’s all about persistence? Patience? Timing? Waiting for your moment? Yes, but not just that.

title: Was Homer’s Ithaca Really an Island?: New Research Challenges a 2,000-Year-Old Assumption
content:
Even if we didn’t make it to a screening of Christopher Nolan’s big-screen adaptation this past summer — and indeed, even if we’ve never read Homer’s original epic at all — we know that the Odyssey tells the story of a ten-year-long journey back to Ithaca. The narrative’s urgency doesn’t arise from the fact that its protagonist, the king Odysseus, has classes at Cornell to teach. In fact, he may not even be trying to get back to the extant Greek island celebrated for bearing that same name. So, at least, argues a recent paper by two distinguished professors, Cambridge’s James Diggle and the University of Aberdeen’s John Underhill. You can read “Was Homer’s Ithaca an Island?” at the online journal Antigone.

Alternatively, you can watch the new video from classicist-novelist Honor Cargill-Martin above. The real Greek island of Ithaca, or Ithaki, with its picturesque hamlets and limestone monoliths, “actually doesn’t match, pretty much at all, the description that Homer gives us of Ithaca,” she says.

title: The Man Who Risked His Life Mocking the Nazis: Read 96 Issues of His Underground Magazine, Created in Hiding During WWII
content:
The word zine, referring to a homemade magazine not distributed through the normal commercial channels, has a longer history than you might expect. Its earliest recorded uses date from 1946 in the world of pulp magazines, most often of the science-fiction variety. But just a year earlier, as it happens, one of the most historically notable zines avant la lettre concluded publication. The end of World War II had everything to do with it, since Het Onderwater-Cabaret, or The Underwater Cabaret, existed as a rebuke against the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. Over its two-year run, it put out 96 issues, totaling over 1,700 pages full of art and poems — all created by one man in hiding in an attic.

Born to a Jewish family in Dortmund in 1908, Curt Bloch studied law with aspirations of becoming a judge. When Hitler rose to power, his plans changed: he first left for Amsterdam, and later, when Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940, he had to keep moving until he ended up in the border town of Enschede.

title: Martin Scorsese Creates a List of 39 Essential Foreign Films for a Young Filmmaker
content:
As a young man, filmmaker Colin Levy got an opportunity of a lifetime. He got a one-on-one meeting with Martin Scorsese. After spending much of his time in high school making a five-minute short, Levy won the national YoungArts award — and, with it, the chance to chat with the guy who directed Goodfellas, Taxi Driver and Raging Bull.

After getting a personal tour of Scorsese’s office and editing bays by none other than legendary editor Thelma Schoonmaker, Levy met the man himself. “It was a defining moment in my path as a filmmaker,” he later wrote on his blog.

title: If Fritz Lang’s Iconic Film Metropolis Had a Kraftwerk Soundtrack
content:
The case of the copyright history of Fritz Lang’s influential sci-fi masterpiece Metropolis is as convoluted as the history of its film print. Lang’s vision and his original almost-three-hour cut were doomed to censorship right from the start. The Nazis took out its more socialist scenes. It’s been edited, colorized, put back together and restored. Wikipedia currently lists nine different versions. Similarly, ownership of the film shifted from distributors back to the public domain, then out of it again, once more of the original footage was rediscovered. And then came 2023, when Metropolis once again landed in the public domain, at least in America. Will we see as many legal battles as new remixes and re-scores? Probably a bit of both.

The film’s original orchestral score is available, but many fans also seek out a score more befitting its futurist origins. Something more electronic.

title: A New Search Engine Lets You Explore 4 Million Works of Art & Historical Photographs from Museums and Libraries Around the World
content: We live in an age when you can describe practically anything you want to see in words, then see it almost immediately. Nobody will ever have laid eyes upon that particular sight before — and quite possibly, nobody ever will again. There we have both the upside and the downside of artificial intelligence-powered image generation. A constant flow of visual, aural, or textual novelty offers stimulation, to put it mildly, but it inevitably comes to feel insubstantial. However complexly derived from the work of humanity it may be, it lacks a direct connection to that work. Not so the results delivered by Arkivism, a new search engine that responds to descriptions by drawing on a collection of more than four million pieces of real art and photography.

title: The San Francisco Public Library Launches a Free Online Archive with 80,000+ Historical Images & Documents to Explore & Download
content: Over 100,000 people move to the San Francisco Bay Area each year. Their motivations for doing so no doubt vary, but these days, the ambition to make a fortune at the epicenter of the tech industry — especially amid the rapidly inflating AI bubble — is hardly unheard of. Unfortunately, that desire can be so all-consuming as to crowd out any interest in, or even curiosity about, the city itself, to say nothing of its wider region. Yet the San Francisco we know today is the result of a story at least 250 years long, very little of which has much to do with venture capital or GPUs. Now, anyone who does want to make a start on understanding it can do so at the new-and-improved platform DigitalSF, with its more than 80,000 historical items available to view and download.

title: Soviet Animations of Winnie the Pooh, Created by the Innovative Animator Fyodor Khitruk
content:
In 1962, the animator Fyodor Khitruk made his directorial debut with Story of One Crime, a film that broke with a Soviet tendency to make imitations of Disney-style animations. The film, as The Guardian explained in its 2012 obituary for the animator, came as a shock. It was stylistically simple and dealt with themes that Disney films would never touch — like, why would a polite clerk murder two housewives with a frying pan?

Khitruk made other films that were packed with social commentary, often taking aim at abuses in the Soviet system. But, he also made straightforward animations for children, none more famous than his series of films based on AA Milne’s beloved Winnie the Pooh books.

Created between 1969 and 1972, Khitruk’s three films star a bear named “Vinni-Pukh” who looks nothing like the Winnie the Pooh that Westerners grew up with. (You can see the original illustrations of Pooh by E.H. Shepard here.) But viewers will certainly recognize the storyline and spirit of the original Pooh in the Soviet adaptations. For decades, these films have enchanted East European viewers, both young and old. And they still occasionally appear on Russian TV.

title: A Beginner’s Guide to Philosophy: From Logic to Epistemology to Metaphysics
content:
These are, perhaps, not the very best times for humanities majors. Seldom do we even hear the once-standard defense that, by pursuing a course of study in subjects of that kind, students “learn how to think.” Such a justification still points to real value, at least in the most demanding settings. Take Harvard’s course Humanities 10, whose digital device-free environment and syllabus covering everything from The Odyssey and Ulysses to Plato and James Baldwin — at a pace of one substantial book per week — recently drew the attention of the Wall Street Journal. Yet it’s always been true that you don’t have to major in anything to learn how to think, or in any case, to make a start of doing so.

Take the philosophy-and-literature YouTuber Jared Henderson, who in the video at the top of the post tells us how he began his self-directed study in high school. “I did what a lot of people would think is natural,” he says. “I went to a bookstore, and then I just found some books that I wanted to read.” The pieces of light reading he took home: Friedrich Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy and Martin Heidegger’s Introduction to Metaphysics.

title: Watch David Bowie Take MTV to Task for Failing to Play Music Videos by Black Artists (1983)
content:
The old vaudeville phrase “Will it play in Peoria?” has its roots in the late 19th century, specifically in Horatio Alger’s novel Five Hundred Dollars; Or Jacob Marlowe’s Secret. Like all of the books Alger wrote extolling the virtues of thrift, study, grooming, industry, etc., this one articulates a middle American bootstraps philosophy and rags-to-riches mythology, while giving the entertainment industry a colorful way to sum up the small-town audiences who embraced Alger’s strait-laced ethic, and who needed to be pandered to or they wouldn’t get all those big-city jokes and references.

Peoria has been many places in the U.S.—from Tulsa to Boise—but whatever the test market, the assumptions have always been the same: the American mainstream is insular, middle class or aspiring to it, culturally conservative, unfailingly white, and fearful of everyone who isn’t. Such demographic dogma has persisted for over a hundred years. Even when it is shown to be outmoded or plain wrong, broadcasters and journalists continue to play to Peoria, genuflecting to a static, populist version of the U.S. that ignores large, rapidly changing segments of the population.
